articles.header: Out of the Cellar: Spatio-temporal Signatures of Rat Sightings in Chicago | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Out of the Cellar: Spatio-temporal Signatures of Rat Sightings in Chicago Research Published: 07 November 2026 Volume 29 , article number 308 ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Edward Helderop 1 & Tony H. Grubesic 1 Abstract Urban rat infestations represent a persistent public health challenge, yet municipal pest management programs often operate reactively and with limited resources. This study applies a suite of spatiotemporal statistical approaches (geographically weighted regression, spatial lag modeling, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting) to predict the spatial distribution of rat sightings across Chicago, Illinois, over a fifteen-year observation window (2011–2025). Using 311 service request data linked to a hexagonal grid (150 m cells) and a set of environmental, demographic, and property-value predictors, we assess the individual and ensemble performance of these models on held-out 2025 rat-sighting data. Our comparative analysis demonstrates that the machine learning frameworks and the spatial lag model generally outperformed geographically weighted regression. Specifically, Random Forest, the spatial lag model, and XGBoost each explained approximately 72% of the variance in rat sighting counts, while the ensemble model achieved the highest overall R 2 (0.73). Variable importance analysis identified recent historical sighting counts as the dominant positive predictor, followed by food establishment density and vacant property rates (both positively associated), and median household income and property values (negatively associated). Spatial hotspot analysis revealed that persistent rat activity hotspots were concentrated in high-density mixed-use corridors characterized by dense commercial food clusters, connected public alleyway infrastructure, and older residential housing stock with elevated vacancy rates. These findings suggest that proactive, data-driven approaches can identify areas in need of resource targeting to create more efficient interventions for cities facing chronic urban rodent challenges. articles.header: Aboveground biomass, carbon stock, and economic valuation of a tiny forest in a small Brazilian City | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Aboveground biomass, carbon stock, and economic valuation of a tiny forest in a small Brazilian City Research Open access Published: 06 November 2026 Volume 29 , article number 307 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Aboveground biomass, carbon stock, and economic valuation of a tiny forest in a small Brazilian City Download PDF Nívea Maria Mafra Rodrigues ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3750-0813 1 , Carem Cristina Araujo Valente ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-1718-1720 2 , Enes Junior Rezende Zanardi ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0003-2214-1840 2 , Marnela da Caridade Manuel ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-1398-8385 2 , Mauricio Ferreira Moreira ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0008-4000-5523 2 , Leonardo Duarte Biazatt ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-9345-8592 2 , Ricardo Pinheiro Cabral ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-4631-2603 2 , Luciélia Lacerda da Silva ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-6994-4734 2 , Amanda Magda Almeida Santos ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-1028-6391 2 , Denyse Cássia de Maria Sales ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6182-0975 2 & … Cristiane Coelho de Moura ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6743-8638 2 Show authors 74 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban forests have gained increasing attention as nature-based solutions, yet quantitative information on aboveground biomass and carbon storage in small urban forest remnants remains limited, particularly in small municipalities. This study aimed to quantify aboveground biomass, carbon stocks, and their illustrative economic valuation in an urban Tiny Forest located in southeastern Brazil. A complete tree inventory was conducted across a 2.76-ha area, including all living trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) ≥ 5 cm. Aboveground biomass was estimated using an allometric equation developed for urban trees, carbon stocks were calculated using a conversion factor of 0.47, and an illustrative economic valuation was derived from a reference price in the voluntary carbon market. The inventory recorded 539 trees belonging to 68 species and 24 botanical families, with native species accounting for 79.0% of the individuals. Total aboveground biomass was estimated at 95.09 Mg (34.45 Mg ha⁻¹), corresponding to 44.69 Mg of carbon (16.19 Mg C ha⁻¹) and 163.88 Mg CO₂e. The illustrative economic valuation of the stored carbon was US$3,349.64. Native species accounted for 86.46% of the estimated carbon stock, with Moquilea tomentosa and Handroanthus impetiginosus among the main contributors. Carbon storage varied with species composition and tree structural characteristics, indicating that abundance alone does not determine species contributions to carbon stocks. These findings demonstrate that small urban forest remnants can represent measurable carbon reservoirs and provide local-scale information to support urban green infrastructure planning. However, the estimates represent carbon stocks at a single point in time and do not establish carbon sequestration rates or potential revenue from certified carbon credits. articles.header: Global urban tree leaf area under climate change: divergent projected trajectories and the limits of space-for-time inference | Urban Ecosystems | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Urban Ecosystems Article Global urban tree leaf area under climate change: divergent projected trajectories and the limits of space-for-time inference Research Open access Published: 06 November 2026 Volume 29 , article number 306 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Urban Ecosystems Aims and scope Submit manuscript Global urban tree leaf area under climate change: divergent projected trajectories and the limits of space-for-time inference Download PDF Gianmarco Goycochea Casas ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-5491-8771 1 52 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban trees moderate city climates, yet how their leaf-area density relates to projected future climates is poorly constrained globally. We fitted a Random Forest model to monthly temperature and precipitation normals and the multi-year mean leaf area index (LAI) derived from a satellite-informed machine-learning urban tree product across 21,590 urban cells, then projected end-of-century change under six Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Leave-one-continent-out validation gave \(R^2 = 0.846\) (95% CI \(0.813\) – \(0.873\) from spatial-block resampling), but that spatial skill does not transfer to time: driven by observed reanalysis anomalies over exactly the satellite record, the same relationship reproduces neither the magnitude nor the pattern of observed change ( \(\rho = +0.087\) ). The response variable is itself a machine-learning product built from overlapping climate predictors, so the spatial fit is not independent evidence of that relationship either. Under modified Mann–Kendall tests with false-discovery-rate control, 19.8% of cells greened and 5.3% browned during 2000–2022, roughly half the browning obtained without those corrections. Global mean change is positive under all scenarios, yet 32.6% of cells decline under SSP5-8.5, with declines concentrated in tropical humid cities and gains at high latitudes. Two further results bound them: 10.6% of cells fall outside the fitted climate domain under SSP5-8.5, and four algorithms agree on the sign of change at only 68.1% of cells. We report these as changes implied by transferring a spatial relationship into future climates, not forecasts: the zonal contrast is the most reproducible result across the evaluated algorithms; cell-level magnitudes and city orderings are not. Murphy ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7670-2469 1 , Peter A. Nelson 2 , Mary Powell 3 & … Josh Gilbert 4 Show authors 13 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban riverscapes contribute substantially to the ecological function, livability, and sustainability of urban and suburban environments, yet their conservation and restoration require assessment approaches that capture interacting ecological, hydrologic, geomorphic, and social dimensions across spatial scales. This article presents URBAN—the Urban Riverscape conditions-Based Assessment for management Needs—as a flexible method for implementing the Technical Domain of the Urban Riverscapes Assessment Framework. URBAN is distinctive in explicitly linking Human Connections and Values with physical processes, community priorities, and anthropogenic stressors that shape long-term riverscape recovery. The assessment is organized around four Facets: Human Connections and Values, Hydrologic Processes and Hydraulic Characteristics, Geomorphic Forms and Processes, and Ecological Structure and Processes. Applied in metropolitan Denver, Colorado, USA, URBAN integrates geospatial analysis, rapid field observations, reach typing, response-potential analysis, and scoring criteria to identify stressors, functional conditions, and management-relevant outcomes. Results from the Denver application indicate that functional conditions and community values may align, diverge, or conflict across reaches, underscoring the need for synthesis across Metrics, Indicators, and Facets rather than reliance on isolated measures. In combination with GIS tools and the broader Urban Riverscape Framework, URBAN provides an objective, multi-scale approach for interpreting multi-causal mechanisms, prioritizing preservation and restoration actions, and supporting planning, regulatory, and engagement needs. The Denver case study demonstrates the utility of URBAN for watershed-scale planning, reach-scale prioritization, and transparent communication among managers, practitioners, and communities, while maintaining adaptability to local context and data availability. Ekwemuka 2 , Deborah Bawa 1 , Monday Christopher 1 , Amobi Anselem Chinweike 1 , Onoja Peter Oche 1 , Faith Jesutofunmi Jeremiah 1 , Ukabiala Maduabuchi Ekeoma 3 & … Unique N. Keke 1 Show authors 9 Accesses 1 Altmetric Explore all metrics Abstract Urban expansion is changing bird assemblages across sub-Saharan Africa, where the sorting of species along urban–rural gradients is understudied. We present a multi-scale analysis of bird assemblages at four locations in Minna, central Nigeria, combining trait-environment modelling, ordination, beta-diversity analysis and machine learning. We recorded 115 species (15 orders, 50 families) in 71 single-visit, 10-minute, fixed-radius point counts (April to July 2021). Because locations were sampled at different times, location and season are partly confounded. Bird detection was weakly predicted (AUC = 0.676): generalists and frugivorous birds were more likely to be detected at multiple stations compared to specialists. Abundance where detected was weakly predicted (R² = 0.133) and higher among seed-eating species. Trait-environment interactions did not improve prediction, indicating trait-associated detection rather than trait-mediated environmental filtering. No community metric was predictable at a withheld location, and no feeding-guild model had predictive skill. Composition differed among locations (PERMANOVA pseudo-F = 1.68, R² = 0.070, p = 0.001), although dispersion also differed and the three locations surveyed within nine days did not differ significantly. Beta-diversity was mostly explained by replacement (0.65) compared to nestedness (0.07). Shannon diversity and functional dispersion were lowest in Gidan Kwano, whereas richness did not differ, even after rarefaction. Composition was associated with tree density, tree size, and elevation, yet not independent from geographic distance. Turnover-driven replacement suggests that networks of habitat patches would provide better protection of regional diversity, which should be confirmed through repeated surveys at same seasons.
